name: Inorganic Chemistry
tagline: Catalysis, coordination compounds, and advanced materials.
seo_title: Inorganic Chemistry — paper summaries, news & innovations | Chemisters
seo_description: Follow Chemisters Inorganic Chemistry on LinkedIn and Facebook: paper summaries, news and innovations in coordination chemistry, main-group and transition-metal chemistry, and solid-state materials.

definition.lead: Inorganic chemistry covers the chemistry of all the elements, with a special focus on metals, minerals and compounds not built around carbon chains.
definition.body: It explains catalysts, pigments, semiconductors, batteries, fertilizers and the metal ions that keep living cells running. From the periodic table to coordination complexes and solid-state materials, it is chemistry's widest map.

facts.label: known elements in the periodic table
Dmitri Mendeleev publishes his periodic table
Nobel Prize to Alfred Werner for coordination chemistry

branches.name: Coordination chemistry
branches.summary: Metal ions surrounded by ligands that donate electron pairs.
branches.example: Cisplatin, a platinum complex used against cancer.

branches.name: Main-group chemistry
branches.summary: The chemistry of the s- and p-block elements.

branches.name: Transition-metal chemistry
branches.summary: d-block metals, their colours, magnetism and redox.
branches.example: Chromium ions give rubies their red colour.

branches.name: Bioinorganic chemistry
branches.example: Iron in haemoglobin, zinc and copper in enzymes.

branches.name: Solid-state chemistry
branches.summary: Structures and properties of extended solids.

branches.name: Lanthanides & actinides
branches.example: Neodymium magnets in motors and wind turbines.

branches.name: Energy materials
branches.summary: Inorganic compounds that store and convert energy.

timeline.title: Oxygen
timeline.text: Joseph Priestley isolates oxygen; Carl Scheele had found it independently.
timeline.why: Opened the way to Lavoisier's new chemistry.

timeline.title: Atomic theory
timeline.text: John Dalton publishes 'A New System of Chemical Philosophy'.
timeline.why: Elements made of atoms with characteristic weights.

timeline.title: The periodic table
timeline.text: Dmitri Mendeleev arranges the elements and leaves gaps for undiscovered ones.
timeline.why: His predicted elements were later found.

timeline.title: Fluorine isolated
timeline.text: Henri Moissan isolates fluorine by electrolysis.
timeline.why: Tamed the most reactive element; Nobel Prize in 1906.

timeline.title: Coordination theory
timeline.text: Alfred Werner explains the structure of metal complexes.

timeline.title: Ferrocene
timeline.text: Ferrocene is discovered; its sandwich structure is worked out in 1952.
timeline.why: Launched modern organometallic chemistry; Nobel Prize in 1973.

timeline.title: Noble gases react
timeline.text: Neil Bartlett makes the first compound of xenon.
timeline.why: Overturned the idea that noble gases are inert.

timeline.title: Cisplatin
timeline.text: Barnett Rosenberg discovers that a platinum compound stops cells dividing.
timeline.why: Became one of the most important cancer drugs.

timeline.title: High-temperature superconductors
timeline.text: Georg Bednorz and Alex Müller discover superconductivity in a copper oxide ceramic.

timeline.title: Row 7 complete
timeline.text: IUPAC names nihonium, moscovium, tennessine and oganesson.
timeline.why: The seventh row of the periodic table is filled.

quiz.q: Who published the periodic table in 1869?
options: Dmitri Mendeleev
John Dalton
Antoine Lavoisier
Niels Bohr
quiz.explain: He left gaps for gallium, scandium and germanium, which were found later.

options: Transition-metal ions whose d-orbitals absorb visible light
Carbon impurities that absorb all light
Heat trapped in the crystal from its formation
Radioactivity that makes the crystal glow
quiz.explain: Chromium makes rubies red and emeralds green, depending on its surroundings.

options: A molecule or ion that donates an electron pair to a metal
A metal atom at the centre of a complex
A proton that binds to a metal
Only a catalyst, never part of a complex
quiz.explain: Water, ammonia and chloride are common ligands.

options: A platinum complex used against cancer
An antibiotic made by soil bacteria
A fertilizer rich in phosphorus
A white pigment used in paints
quiz.explain: It binds DNA and stops cancer cells dividing.

options: Oxygen
Nitrogen
Glucose
Sodium
quiz.explain: Each haemoglobin carries up to four O₂ molecules.

quiz.q: What happened in 1962 to the idea that noble gases are inert?
options: Neil Bartlett made a xenon compound
Helium caught fire
Argon formed water
Radon exploded
quiz.explain: Many xenon compounds are now known.

quiz.q: What is the structure of ferrocene?
options: An iron atom sandwiched between two five-membered carbon rings
A chain of iron atoms linked by carbon
A cube of iron atoms with carbon on the faces
Iron oxide with carbon trapped inside

quiz.q: What is the coordination number of the cobalt in [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺?
quiz.explain: Six ammonia ligands surround the cobalt octahedrally.

quiz.q: Which element did Henri Moissan isolate in 1886?
options: Fluorine
Chlorine
Sodium
Uranium
quiz.explain: Many chemists before him were injured trying.

quiz.q: Lanthanides such as neodymium are used in…
options: Strong permanent magnets
Table salt
Window glass only
Fertilizers
quiz.explain: Neodymium–iron–boron magnets power motors and wind turbines.

quiz.q: Why are many transition-metal compounds coloured while zinc compounds are usually white?
options: Zn²⁺ has a full d¹⁰ shell, so no d–d transitions
Zinc is too heavy to absorb visible light
Zinc compounds are gases at room temperature
Zinc is radioactive, which bleaches colour
quiz.explain: Colour needs electrons that can jump between d orbitals.

quiz.q: How many elements are known today?
quiz.explain: The heaviest, oganesson, was named in 2016.
